These findings highlight the potential of keystroke dynamics as real-time indicators of cognitive effort during LLM prompting, while also showing their limitations in capturing perceived collaboration success.

2611.31025.title: Token Pruning Needs a Protected Sink Token: Coherent Spatial Aggregation in Vision Transformers
2611.31025.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are a predominant architecture for computer vision, with token reduction emerging as a popular paradigm to improve their efficiency. Prior work compares reduction algorithms, but not how models respond to them, nor how their response changes with model depth. We propose Monte Carlo Token Pruning (MCTP), which estimates each token's impact on the prediction when tokens are explicitly removed during the forward pass. Applying MCTP to recent pretrained models, we observe that most, such as DINOv3, maintain a similar ranking of token importance at every depth (high Coherent Aggregation), while SigLIP 2 does not. This coherence requires predictions to survive pruning, which depends on keeping high-norm "sink" tokens: prefix tokens are kept by design, while prefix-free SigLIP 2 forms them on patch tokens, which pruning may remove. We show that in removing DINOv3's prefix tokens, its predictions and coherence collapse, while protecting only 5 tokens for SigLIP 2 cuts the token impact outside the object's bounding box by up to 62%. Beyond this, MCTP offers a post-hoc method to evaluate how a pretrained ViT responds to pruning, and suggests that token reduction methods should keep "sinks".

2611.31021.title: Parsing Visual Latents for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
2611.31021.abstract: Spatial reasoning across multiple views requires inferring the 3D relations between objects and the camera from 2D observations, which depends on cross-view correspondence and scene geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) do not reliably extract. Pretrained vision encoders already capture this information in their latent features, with CLIP linking objects to image regions, DINOv3 matching semantics across views, and VGGT encoding multi-view geometry. However, VLMs do not benefit from these features when we present them directly in context as grayscale feature images. We therefore propose LatentParse, a training-free framework that parses latent features into explicit spatial evidence for VLMs. In LatentParse, an analyst VLM probes the features of all three encoders with predefined tools that locate objects, track them across views, and measure motion between views. It then distills the results into a concise text report, which is provided together with the images to the VLM to answer the question. We evaluate LatentParse on MMSI-Bench, MV-RoboBench and SPAR-Bench, where it improves all five VLMs over the photo-only baseline by 0.7-2.4 percentage points on average. On MMSI-Bench, it raises Qwen3.8-27B from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest improvements of 19.2 percentage points on the camera-related questions. These results suggest that latent features become useful for spatial reasoning once they are parsed into relation evidence, without training. Code is available at https://github.com/Harvard-AI-and-Robotics-Lab/LatentParse.

2611.30725.title: Co-speech Gesture Attribute Annotation with 3D Human Mesh Recovery
2611.30725.abstract: Co-speech gestures convey meaning alongside speech, but annotating their physical attributes in video is labour-intensive. We propose two approaches to automate annotation of ten gesture attributes using human mesh recovery (HMR), which estimates a full 3D body skeleton from a single video frame: AI-assisted geometrical rules and a graph convolutional network (SL-GCN). Both use pose estimates from SAM 3D Body, evaluated on 2,020 gestures from the GESRes dataset. For physically defined attributes such as height, arm swivel and movement speed, both methods achieve agreement with expert annotation comparable to that between human annotators. For attributes whose annotation requires higher-level multimodal contextual inference, performance remains lower. The rule-based approach requires substantially less annotated data, is fully transparent, and can be adapted to different annotation schemes, offering a practical and interpretable complement to data-driven methods

2611.30646.title: Part-wise Certified State Estimation of Articulated Objects from Passive Stereo
2611.30646.abstract: Robots in manufacturing often handle thin, hinged objects known from CAD models that change shape during the task, like folding cartons. Monitoring such tasks requires estimating the object's articulation state, its pose and the shape of any semi-deformable part. Learning-based estimators generalise across objects but lose precision while handling thin parts. Model-based fitting is precise but often needs accurate depth, a close initial estimate and a clean object mask. We present part-wise certification of an articulated object's state, estimated from passive stereo. Our estimator rivals the precision of the best model-based fitting method without using depth, a close initial estimate or a mask. We detect the corners that the CAD model defines in both stereo images and fit the articulated model to them. Geometric certificates, which we extend from rigid to articulated objects, then tell whether to trust each part, because the fit returns a state even for hidden parts. Certified estimates on unlabelled video become labels that improve sim-to-real transfer. On five of seven simulated objects, we locate the parts we certify three to five times more precisely than the strongest learned baseline on the same readings, given depth and true masks. On a real folding carton, our median corner error on the end panels is 2.1% of the carton's size, at least 40% lower than every learned baseline and also lower than a depth-based fit initialised near the true state.

2611.30564.title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models
2611.30564.abstract: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.

2611.30514.title: When Do Spatial Plans Help Text-to-Image Generation? Causal Control, System Utility, and Text Responsiveness
2611.30514.abstract: A generator can follow a spatial plan, but the benefit of supplying that plan depends on what the model can already do from text. In a controlled study with 18 paired training seeds, correcting predicted positions and sizes improves spatial intersection-over-union by 0.030, yet direct text is non-inferior at matched training compute. In a pretrained generator, a fixed rule layout improves two-object task success over the same text-only adapter by 12.50 percentage points, mostly by separating objects that already appear in the correct order. We then ask whether a more precise instruction can achieve the same separation across conditioning paths. On 288 new task families, adding a minimum-gap instruction improves success by 37.15 points with the text-only adapter, by at most 0.69 points with widely spaced regions, and by 6.94 points with tightly spaced regions. Under tight regions, 230 of 288 baseline images have the correct objects and direction yet miss the required gap, ruling out a high baseline success rate as the sole explanation for the weak text response.

2611.30424.title: Spatial-Zero: Self-Evolving Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models from Zero Data
2611.30424.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires a vision-language model~(VLM) to understand metric distances, three-dimensional relationships, and viewpoint-dependent geometry. Learning these capabilities typically requires externally curated training data. This paper introduces Spatial-Zero, a VLMs' training framework that can self-evolve through autonomous spatial exploration with zero data. Spatial-Zero addresses two key challenges in autonomous spatial exploration: reliably generating valid spatial interaction tasks and providing accurate supervision for learning from these tasks. Specifically, a proposer specifies object configurations and questions, and a Coder turns them into executable scene programs that produce multi-view images and explicit scene geometry. A Geometric Oracle checks spatial constraints, visibility, and answer uniqueness and derives ground-truth labels from executed geometry; these labels supervise the Solver and ground difficulty feedback, while validation outcomes guide subsequent task generation. Across six spatial reasoning benchmarks and three VLM backbones, Spatial-Zero yields consistent gains through iterative self-evolution. After three iterations, Qwen3.5-9B improves average accuracy by 3.23 percentage points; with Qwen3.5-4B, Spatial-Zero also outperforms existing VLM self-evolution methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/YutongLi2024/Spatial-Zero

2611.30215.title: Benchmarking Geospatial Foundation Models under Calibrated Label Errors
2611.30215.abstract: Earth-observation labels from maps, older products or hurried annotation arrive misaligned, coarse, loosely outlined or incomplete. Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are nevertheless benchmarked with labels taken as correct. A practitioner therefore cannot tell which encoder to choose when the labels are imperfect. We present a benchmark protocol for fine-tuning under such labels. Four spatially structured error types are calibrated to equal label mIoU and applied identically to every model and seed. Every contrast is paired and read against an equivalence margin of $\pm 3$ points and a minimum detectable effect. We apply it to nine encoders, six decoder heads and ten datasets. In an exploratory reading at a matched learning rate the satellite-pretrained and web-pretrained DINOv3 encoders are equivalent within the margin on 8 of 9 datasets. Multispectral GFMs and an ImageNet ResNet-50 are equivalent within the margin on about half of them. Labels with random offsets cost the least at equal label quality. Under other decoder heads the verdicts mostly hold on FLAIR-2 and are decoder dependent on HLS Burn Scars. On four of five real label pairs the real label costs more than its matched simulated type. No choice of pretraining data makes an encoder consistently more robust, so the encoder is better chosen by its accuracy under imperfect labels.

2611.30012.title: FlexGaze: Weakly Supervised Gaze Estimation at Scale
2611.30012.abstract: Most gaze estimation models are trained on data collected using specialized equipment. The limited diversity of subjects, scenes, and head poses in these datasets hinders generalization to new conditions. We present FlexGaze, a family of 3D gaze estimators pretrained with weak supervision from gaze labels (pseudo-labels) automatically generated from in-the-wild images. We use off-the-shelf models to predict 2D gaze targets and scene depth, then combine these predictions to generate 3D gaze labels for approximately 3.24 million head instances. At inference, FlexGaze predicts gaze from a head crop alone and can handle profile and rear views without requiring face detection or head pose estimation. We use data augmentation during training to improve robustness to variations in crop position and scale. Pretrained using only these generated gaze labels, FlexGaze generalizes to unseen benchmarks. After supervised fine-tuning on public gaze datasets, we evaluate FlexGaze on eight benchmarks under a unified evaluation protocol. Our models match or outperform publicly available gaze estimators with several times as many parameters on most benchmarks. We release our dataset of generated gaze labels, all trained models, and code via https://github.com/ihp-lab/FlexGaze.

2611.29421.title: A colour-marker tracker for pose estimation of slender surgical instruments: vision-language-model-guided adaptive colour calibration
2611.29421.abstract: Slender surgical instruments need small, narrow markers for camera-based pose estimation. A colour-stripe marker fits this requirement, but its colours in the image drift from the design values with lighting, printing and camera settings. Because the colours can only be corrected after the marker has been found, methods that rely on the design colours face a circular problem. We propose vision-language-model (VLM)-based adaptive colour calibration and compare it with two rule-based methods, which re-measure the colours from detections made with the design colours: Initial colour update does so once after tracking starts, and Colour adaptation continuously during tracking. VLM guidance uses a fine-tuned VLM to find the markers without relying on the design colours and builds the colour profile from their pixels. Recall/F1 (%) for Initial colour update, Colour adaptation and VLM guidance were 92.0/95.7, 87.8/93.3 and 98.2/99.1 on 672 synthetic image pairs; 51.3/67.2, 48.8/65.0 and 83.8/87.0 on eight degraded laboratory videos; and 38.9/55.2, 19.7/29.7 and 100/100 on a surgical-robot (da Vinci) video with strongly shifted colours. In that video the rule-based methods never found the purple/cyan marker, whereas VLM guidance found all 234 markers with no false positives. In a simulation, the hue boundary between the two stripes moved by less than 0.1 pixel for exposure gains of 0.5-2.0, compared with 2.9-4.0 pixels for a boundary found with a fixed brightness threshold. When the degradation is mild, the rule-based methods, which need no training and no GPU, are sufficient. When the colours change greatly, the gain comes from a VLM-guided candidate search that does not rely on the design colours. Combining colour-stripe markers with adaptive colour calibration enables tracking of slender surgical instruments with small markers.

2611.29341.title: MIMORPHEUS: Rethinking Cross-Modal Supervision for Human Pose Estimation from Radar Signals
2611.29341.abstract: Deep learning has shown promise for estimating human pose with multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar through walls. Building paired radar and pose datasets demands considerable time and manual effort, while large visual pose datasets provide no corresponding radar echoes. Physical simulation can supply synthetic signals, but requires expertise in scattering models and can leave a gap between simulated and real data. To address this challenge, we introduce MIMORPHEUS, a framework that generates radar echoes from 3D human poses through conditional diffusion. To prepare echo and pose representations, MIMO-VAE compresses the echoes according to their channel and fast time sample structure, while SkeleCoder learns pose features through contrastive alignment with echo features. These pose features then guide diffusion in the MIMO-VAE latent space, and the VAE decoder reconstructs echoes from the generated latents. Once trained, the generator augments radar data by producing different echoes for a recorded pose and supplies the radar modality for pose annotations in existing visual datasets. In data augmentation experiments, our method reduces MPJPE by 6.8%-11.2% across four radar pose estimators. Transfer experiments with three public pose datasets also show that visual pose annotations can supply useful radar training data. Code will be made publicly available on GitHub.

2611.29330.title: SKIA: Spatial-Knowledge Informed Attention for Robust Remote Photoplethysmography under Lower-Face Motion Artifacts
2611.29330.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables contactless physiological monitoring from facial videos, but facial motion, particularly mouth and jaw movements during cognitive and communicative tasks, can severely degrade signal reconstruction. We present SKIA, a lightweight, mask-guided framework that suppresses motion-prone lower-face regions while preserving physiological cues from the forehead and cheeks. Using the UBFC-rPPG benchmark, we first investigate static lower-face suppression in the classical CHROM pipeline. Static masking improves waveform Pearson correlation from 0.3507 to 0.4166 (p < 0.001) and reduces heart-rate mean absolute error (MAE) from 33.50 to 23.44 bpm. Building on this finding, we introduce SKIA-Net, a compact spatiotemporal architecture that combines raw facial frames, statically masked representations, and temporal motion differences to reconstruct blood volume pulse (BVP) waveforms. The full model achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.7522 and a heart-rate MAE of 3.73 bpm on UBFC-rPPG, outperforming single-stream variants. Ablation studies show that the static mask provides complementary information to raw appearance and that static anatomical priors outperform the tested dynamic optical-flow-based masking strategy. These results suggest that spatially informed, temporally stable masking can improve motion-robust rPPG estimation. Code: https://github.com/lee-vtruong/SKIA-rPPG

2611.29282.title: RadioWorld: Transferring World Models to Radio-Frequency Radiance Fields
2611.29282.abstract: Electromagnetic (EM) wave propagation in the physical world constitutes a Radio-Frequency (RF) radiance field, providing rich information for 6G communication and sensing. However, existing neural RF field methods suffer from three fundamental limitations: (1) they predominantly rely on per-scene optimization and cannot generalize to unseen scenes; (2) they require costly reference RF measurements in each target scene; and (3) they degrade severely when extrapolating beyond the vicinity of reference measurements. To overcome these limitations, we present RadioWorld, a general framework that adapts a world model to synthesize RF radiance fields directly from physical scene geometry and transceiver locations, without requiring any reference RF measurements at inference. Specifically, RadioWorld couples two specialized modules within a dual-stream Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture: a Scene-Understanding Transformer that encodes 3D scene geometry and transceiver locations to extract environment-aware global EM propagation features, and a Field-Generation Transformer that attends to these features to synthesize the RF radiance field with the local query conditions. We also establish UrbanRF-Bench, a large-scale ray-traced benchmark spanning 657 urban scenes and 32,850 RF radiance fields across seven global cities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RadioWorld significantly outperforms specialized baselines and accurately synthesizes RF fields at arbitrary locations in unseen cities. Code, datasets, and checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.

2611.29168.title: SpatialDuet: Bayesian task routing between a metric expert and a geometry expert for spatial intelligence
2611.29168.abstract: Embodied assistants and wearable devices need 3D spatial reasoning, and their limited hardware restricts them to small vision-language models (VLMs). Small spatial VLMs acquire different abilities from their training: a model trained on large spatial question sets estimates object and room sizes well, whereas a model with a 3D geometry encoder is better at relative directions and absolute distances. Instead of training a single model for all spatial tasks, as published methods do, we build one system that uses each frozen model for the tasks it handles best. We propose SpatialDuet, which pairs a metric expert with a geometry expert under a Bayesian task router. The metric expert is a data-driven spatial VLM run with three training-free modules: training-aligned sampling, metric-aware minimum Bayes risk decoding and per-type metric calibration. The geometry expert is a VLM with a 3D geometry encoder. For each question type, the router estimates from labelled development questions how likely each expert is to be better, and pools their answers with that probability as weight, in log space for numeric answers and over the option distributions for multiple-choice answers. Extensive experiments on four spatial benchmarks covering video and single images validate SpatialDuet; it outperforms the best published small VLMs by 3.17% on VSI-Bench and, excluding a model trained on CV-Bench-style data, by 1.44% on CV-Bench, without training any model weight.

2611.29146.title: RVLM: Fewer Tokens, Better Resolution Scaling, Fine-Grained Spatial Grounding
2611.29146.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) tokenize images using fixed spatial grids, so visual token count grows with pixel area rather than scene content. We propose to group neighboring patches based on their visual appearance, allowing tokens to represent coherent image regions rather than fixed spatial windows. We introduce RVLM, a VLM trained to use regions rather than patches as its visual units. Analyzing region construction for general-purpose VLMs, we find that regions must cover the full image, stay spatially connected during end-to-end training, and preserve fine structure such as small text, while semantic grouping adds little. RVLM therefore partitions images using training-free Felzenszwalb-Huttenlocher segmentation, assigns each ViT patch to a region, and pools patches within each region into a variable-length sequence of visual tokens. The patch-to-region assignment is retained to support spatially precise prediction through coarse-to-fine decoding. Across tasks spanning VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation, RVLM matches or improves example-weighted task performance while using 21.5% fewer visual tokens than an identically trained patch baseline. The advantage grows with image resolution, reaching a 5.3-point gain while using 51.8% fewer visual tokens at the highest-resolution setting. The gains are largest on spatially demanding tasks, where prior token-reduction methods degrade most sharply. RVLM adds no model parameters and improves inference throughput by up to 35.9%. On unseen pathology and satellite images and on video benchmarks without any video training, RVLM performs on par with the patch baseline while using 2-3$\times$ fewer visual tokens. These results establish regions as a scalable alternative to patch-based visual representations while preserving the spatial precision required for grounded prediction.

2611.28979.title: AlignHand: Multi-View Hand Reconstruction from a Frozen Monocular Prior
2611.28979.abstract: Modern monocular hand estimators recover detailed 3D meshes from individual images, yet effectively leveraging their predictions across multiple views remains challenging. Independently predicted meshes can disagree in scale, placement, and articulation, limiting the integration of complementary multi-view information. Hence, we present AlignHand, a calibrated multi-view framework that builds on a frozen monocular hand reconstruction prior to align and enhance its predictions. Specifically, AlignHand refines cross-view joint observations and estimates their reliability to establish a shared metric reference for alignment. Once the meshes are brought into a common frame, their complementary surface evidence is selectively fused across anatomical regions, followed by pixel-aligned refinement that predicts bounded residual displacements from local image features. This global-to-local integration enables AlignHand to exploit complementary observations while preserving the strong monocular prior. Extensive experiments on DexYCB-MV, HanCo, and HO3D-Eval-MV demonstrate that AlignHand achieves the lowest MPVPE and MPJPE among the compared methods under the respective evaluation protocols, reducing MPVPE by 30.1%, 29.1%, and 8.0%, respectively, compared with a matched geometry baseline.

2611.28913.title: From Dense to Sparse: Morton-Ordered Sparse Mapping for Efficient 3D Mesh Generation
2611.28913.abstract: Unified 3D understanding and generation require compact sequences preserving spatial structure. Dense grids yield long sequences, while serialization can separate spatial neighbors. We propose Sparse Proximity Aware Compression (SPAC), a shared sparse SDF vocabulary combining sparse encoding with reversible spatial merging. A Sparse SDF VQ-VAE quantizes near-surface features while retaining explicit coordinates, using reconstruction supervision for surface fidelity and detail. 3D Byte-Pair Encoding (3D-BPE) merges recurring face-adjacent patterns using relative offsets before serialization. Macro tokens expand exactly into leaf tokens and coordinates. After Morton serialization, a shared LLM reads geometry for captioning and predicts tokens that decode into meshes for text-conditioned generation. With fixed geometry, architecture, and band width in voxels, sparse encoder cost grows approximately quadratically with resolution. 3D-BPE reduces mean complete LLM sequence length by 45.4 percent, including coordinates, text, and control tokens. SPAC achieves strong results in both 3D captioning and text-conditioned mesh generation. Ablations show gains over leaf tokens and Morton 1D-BPE in both tasks. The project page at https://yangjj007.github.io/spac/ .

2611.28839.title: Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead for Vision-Language-Action Models
2611.28839.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings.

2611.28670.title: Learning Continuous Scene Depth Representations via Cross-Modal Gaussian Rendering
2611.28670.abstract: Depth super-resolution with color guidance is a fundamental problem in geometric scene understanding that aims to reconstruct high-resolution depth using structural cues from color images. In practical RGB-D systems, the resolution gap between depth and color images often varies, requiring flexible upsampling factors. However, many existing methods are designed for predefined integer scales. Although implicit methods support arbitrary-scale reconstruction, they typically rely on computationally demanding per-pixel neural decoding and may struggle to recover sharp depth boundaries and fine structures. To this end, we propose a cross-modal Gaussian rendering framework that learns continuous depth representations for arbitrary-scale depth super-resolution. Specifically, we first construct hierarchical Gaussian representations for progressive depth reconstruction, with explicit spatial support defined by learnable Gaussian primitives. Building on this representation, we design a Structure-Aware Gaussian Aggregation module that combines spatial weights with cross-modal feature affinities to reduce aggregation across depth discontinuities. We then develop a Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Rendering module that adapts Gaussian spatial kernels to the target pixel footprint. To further facilitate cross-modal learning, we propose a training strategy that gradually introduces higher-frequency guidance information during training. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method at both in-distribution and out-of-distribution upsampling scales.

2611.28665.title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
2611.28665.abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.

2611.28649.title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
2611.28649.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

2611.28646.title: OrthoLatentCAD: Orthographic Spatial Latents for Hand-Drawn CAD Program Generation
2611.28646.abstract: Freehand orthographic drawings capture early design intent, yet recovering executable sketch--extrude CAD programs from raster front, right, and top views remains challenging: noisy, dimension-free 2D layouts must be reconciled into an ordered construction history. We introduce Hand2CAD, a benchmark of 215K ABC-derived synthetic orthographic-drawing--CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets drawn by CAD-trained participants. Recovering CAD programs from orthographic drawings requires both cross-view geometric reasoning and alignment between visual features and program representations. We propose OrthoLatentCAD to address these two challenges. It fuses local geometry with global context on canonical planes, exchanges evidence between paired plane lines indexed by the same shared-axis coordinate, and maps the spatial representation to ordered program latents through queries inherited from a frozen CAD autoencoder. Across the evaluated one- to three-view configurations, OrthoLatentCAD outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity while benefiting from additional views. Without real-data fine-tuning, it also outperforms the baselines on held-out real drawings. We will release the dataset, code, and evaluation scripts.

2611.28283.title: HandXFM: Semantic-Structural Distillation for Hand Radiograph Foundation Models
2611.28283.abstract: Hand radiographs support diverse clinical tasks, including skeletal maturity assessment, rheumatoid arthritis scoring, abnormality screening, and anatomical localization, yet existing models are typically trained separately for each task and dataset. We present HandXFM, a domain-specific foundation model that leverages cross-modality knowledge for comprehensive hand X-ray understanding. HandXFM distills semantic priors from BiomedCLIP and structural cues from a chest X-ray Vision Transformer (ViT) through a unified alignment framework, integrating complementary medical knowledge in an interpretable way. After pretraining, HandXFM can be adapted to a range of musculoskeletal tasks, including bone age estimation, SvH score prediction, abnormality detection, joint localization, bone segmentation, and visual question answering. It consistently outperforms task-specific and single-expert baselines, achieving up to 0.11 improvement in Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) for bone age prediction and a 12\% accuracy gain in abnormality classification. Moreover, HandXFM generalizes to unseen datasets and yields cross-attention maps linking clinical terms to anatomical regions. These results demonstrate that multi-expert distillation effectively unifies semantic and structural supervision within a single pretrained model, establishing HandXFM as an interpretable and generalizable foundation model for hand radiograph analysis.

2611.28193.title: FastD4RT: Training-Free Acceleration of Dynamic 4D Reconstruction and Tracking
2611.28193.abstract: Query-based 4D reconstruction models such as D4RT encode a video once into a global scene representation and obtain outputs by decoding independent point queries. However, inference is often influenced by dense outputs and long videos. Although D4RT separates encoding from decoding, a dense output still requires one decoder query for every pixel of every frame, and a long video is still encoded as many overlapping segments. In this work, we analyze the inference cost of D4RT and show that a large part of it is redundant. In particular, we find that the later decoder blocks attend to a small set of tokens shared by all queries. Based on these findings, we propose FastD4RT, a training-free framework that accelerates D4RT. By exploiting the smoothness of the outputs over time and across pixels, FastD4RT encodes and decodes only at sparse anchors and recovers the remaining outputs via interpolation. It decodes the remaining queries against a shared token set selected once per segment. We further characterize the errors introduced by both components. Experimental results show that FastD4RT accelerates D4RT by about 5 times on average across all its tasks with competitive accuracy, and further improves accuracy on long videos. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lycheemeng/fastd4rt.

2611.30963.title: Foresight Forcing: Learning Spatial Foresight for Robotic Manipulation
2611.30963.abstract: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing ($\mathcal{F}^{2}$), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, $\mathcal{F}^{2}$ achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.

2611.29874.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
2611.29874.abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

2611.29494.title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines
2611.29494.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

2611.28793.title: STAC++: Plug-and-Play Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Aware Cache Compression for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
2611.28793.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC's fixed-resolution spatial key-value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

2611.28185.title: SAMA: Training-Free Consensus Ridge Tracking for Camera-Based Heart Rate on Five Public Datasets
2611.28185.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is usually benchmarked by one heart rate per video, a figure that hides the short windows in which a tele-consultation would actually read the pulse. We present SAMA, a training-free estimator that (i) forms a quality-weighted consensus of POS and CHROM chrominance spectra, (ii) discounts frequencies occupied by pulse-free references derived from the same frames (frame motion, skin-mask geometry and background brightness), (iii) follows the heart rate through time with a Viterbi ridge under a random-walk prior, and (iv) returns a track-filtered, amplitude-normalised waveform with a per-window confidence. No parameter is learned and no dataset-specific tuning is used. On 218 recordings from 111 participants in five public datasets (UBFC-rPPG, PURE, SUMS, M3PD and a two-participant subset of MMPD), all processed with the same fixed face box and scored with a re-implementation of the rPPG-Toolbox protocol, SAMA has the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) averaged over datasets at every protocol level: 4.40 against 5.13,bpm for POS per video, 4.80 against 5.43 on 30,s windows and 5.05 against 6.59 on 10,s windows. Pooled over participants, the bootstrap interval of its paired difference from POS excludes zero on 30,s and 10,s windows (Wilcoxon p=0.11 and 0.004) but not per video, and it does not beat POS on SUMS per video or on the MMPD subset. Withholding the 20\% least confident windows lowers the pooled 10,s error from 4.06 to 2.33,bpm. We also show that the per-video protocol has a floor of 1.2--1.6,bpm on datasets where heart rate drifts, and that skin tone cannot be recovered from uncalibrated video, which motivates the instrumented, skin-tone-stratified collection we propose for the Indian population. The method does not surpass the best published neural networks on UBFC-rPPG; we report where it stands against them without re-running them.

2611.30629.title: Faster, Smaller, and Better-Looking: Fast-GSVC for 2D Gaussian Video Coding
2611.30629.abstract: 2D Gaussians have emerged as a promising explicit representation for videos. However, fitting Gaussians to a video sequence requires substantial computation, resulting in long encoding times. In this work, we present Fast-GSVC, a 2D Gaussian video codec that accelerates encoding while improving rate-distortion performance. We identify the key bottlenecks in 2DGS training and accelerate optimization through improved initialization, smoother yet more aggressive parameter updates, coarse-to-fine progressive Gaussian optimization, and optical-flow guidance for both Gaussian initialization and temporal propagation. We also discovered that the quantization fine-tuning process of the existing codec does not fully exploit temporal coherence between frames, leading to suboptimal compression. To address this, we preserve spatiotemporal correlations to maintain concentrated residuals and introduce temporal-aware quantization for further improved rate-distortion performance. In our experiments on the UVG dataset, Fast-GSVC reduces encoding time by up to 92.5%, corresponding to a 13.4X speedup over GSVC. At comparable PSNR, it reduces file size by up to 58%; at comparable bit-per-pixel, it improves PSNR by up to 2.5 dB. Project page: https://longanwang-cs.github.io/fastgsvc/.

2611.30166.title: Toward Open Room-Scale Scanning with Consumer LiDAR via Depth-Inertial Odometry
2611.30166.abstract: Room scanning with consumer LiDAR today depends on ARKit, whose tracking and map update are a black box: an application receives depth and poses but cannot inspect how they were produced, so an error in a scan cannot be traced to its cause. This paper examines whether an open alternative, one whose every stage can be inspected, is feasible on the device. Mobile-LIO is a depth-inertial odometry pipeline that uses the phone's depth and inertial data and no ARKit poses. On seven ScanNet++ iPhone recordings it completed every scene with 0.2-2.0 m deviation from the ARKit-derived reference, where six open-source LiDAR-inertial estimators run as configured for dedicated scanners had at least 4.46 m in 41 of 42 runs (two of the six also failed a noise-free adapter check, and Mobile-LIO has a speed cap they lack; the comparison is not controlled and does not rone 15 Pro Max, a buildwith corrected phone code kept up with the sensor in 14 of 15 replay runs of three 7-13 s recordings; e estimator before thosecorrections. 2611.29912.title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
2611.29912.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.

2611.29748.title: Performance Evaluation of Nonlinear Model Predictive and Sliding Mode Controllers on a 4-Cable Spatial CSPR in Simscape
2611.29748.abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR) actuated by four cables. The robot is modeled in two parallel ways: (i) via an analytical dynamic model with included cable elasticity and frictional losses, and (ii) in MATLAB Simscape Multibody, capturing realistic physical effects. Both controllers are implemented under identical reference trajectories, system constraints, and tuning strategies. Our results show that NMPC achieves superior tracking accuracy and stronger disturbance rejection compared to SMC, but at the cost of higher computational demand. Moreover, both controllers were tested on an analytical model of the robot and a Simscape model. The close agreement between the two, for both control schemes, confirms the accuracy of the analytical formulation and its consistency with the physics-based simulation. The study highlights the value of physics-based simulation as a complementary tool for validating advanced controllers under realistic conditions, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.

2611.28707.title: IRIS: Inverse Dynamics from Random Exploration with Eye-in-hand Sensing
2611.28707.abstract: Imagine-then-execute methods offer a promising paradigm for video-based manipulation, where a video planner predicts future visual subgoals and an inverse dynamics model (IDM) grounds them into robot actions. Despite their promise, these methods remain limited by action grounding. First, the IDM is typically trained on limited task-specific demonstrations and can generalize poorly even when given oracle visual subgoals, indicating that action grounding remains a bottleneck beyond visual planning errors. Second, precise execution benefits from eye-in-hand observations, but eye-in-hand video planning is both hard to learn and hard to scale: the viewpoint moves with the robot, and such videos are scarce at internet scale. To overcome these challenges, we propose IRIS, a video-based manipulation framework that learns a highly generalizable, execution-aware IDM. First, IRIS scales action grounding by pretraining the IDM on task-agnostic random exploration data, which provides diverse visual state transitions paired with robot actions without human task annotation. Second, it extends the IDM with eye-in-hand sensing through a two-stage training scheme, without requiring eye-in-hand video planning. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show that IRIS improves action grounding and data efficiency, enables more precise execution, and achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art manipulation policies.

2611.28274.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
2611.28274.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.

2611.31215.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
2611.31215.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

2611.30226.title: VeriWorld: A Verifiable Visual SWE-Bench for Spatial Reasoning in 3D Environments
2611.30226.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for spatial tasks such as navigation and manipulation, where they must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input in order to act correctly. Existing benchmarks usually test perception and reasoning in isolation, making it hard to tell whether failures come from visual understanding, downstream reasoning, or the bridge between them. We introduce VeriWorld, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with executable actions and deterministic verification. For task families where all three channels are well-defined, we evaluate matched visual, structured, and combined input conditions on the same instance, environment, and verifier; families without a clean visual/structured/combined split are reported separately. This design supports controlled comparisons of perception, reasoning, and their interaction. Using this setup, we uncover two diagnostic findings. First, models often perform much better when task-relevant information, such as object identity, current state, or target location, is given explicitly than when it must be read from the rendered scene, revealing a recurring visual-to-structure gap. Second, action-space and harness design can change outcomes even under the same task and information condition, showing that interaction protocol is itself a confounding variable. VeriWorld is open-sourced to support reproducible and fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.

2611.30131.title: iFeST: An Iterative Motion Correction Framework for Fetal Brain Diffusion MRI via Frequency-Spatial-Temporal Modeling
2611.30131.abstract: Fetal brain diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a pivotal non-invasive tool for assessing the development of brain connectivity and microstructure. However, the prolonged acquisition times and complex sampling requirements render dMRI highly susceptible to unpredictable fetal motion. Existing motion correction methods typically process each dMRI volume independently and focus on inter-slice motion. Such strategies fail to utilize the coherent information between dMRI volumes along different diffusion directions and lack the ability to restore the intra-slice corruption. To address these limitations, we proposed iFeST, an iterative framework that combines frequency (k-space), spatial, and temporal (inter-slice) modeling for fetal brain dMRI motion correction. At each iteration, iFeST integrates information across diffusion directions into fiber orientation distributions (FODs). These distributions encode local fiber orientations within each voxel and serve as microstructural priors for intra-slice restoration and inter-slice alignment in the next iteration. To train the framework, we developed a fetal brain dMRI motion simulator that synthesizes compound motion artifacts from FODs. Evaluation on simulated datasets demonstrated that iFeST outperformed four inter-slice networks in motion estimation and three intra-slice networks in image restoration. Further validation on a real-world dataset confirmed significantly better volume reconstruction and FOD estimation than conventional pipelines. Overall, iFeST provides a learning-based framework for fetal dMRI motion correction, restoring motion-corrupted data and improving microstructural reconstruction for downstream diagnostic applications.

2611.30436.title: MF-EDA: Joining Membership Functions to Adapt the Number of Distributions in Gaussian Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms
2611.30436.abstract: An estimation-of-distribution algorithm (EDA) usually samples from one Gaussian, whose peak sits where most selected individuals are. On a landscape with two funnels that is not where the best solutions are: the wider funnel supplies most of the selected individuals, and the deeper funnel, which holds the global optimum, is lost early. This paper builds the search distribution as a neuro-fuzzy system builds a model: from Gaussian membership functions joined by membership degrees. In every generation the proposed MF-EDA searches the principal directions of the selected individuals for the direction along which they are bimodal, describes them on that direction by one or two membership functions according to the Bayesian information criterion and a separation test, joins each membership function to a local Gaussian in the other directions, and samples from the normalised union. A membership function has height one whatever the number of individuals under it, so a detected funnel receives samples according to its width. A two-region selection model shows that sampling shares proportional to the head count, as in a Gaussian mixture, compound the early disadvantage of the deeper funnel, and that the union does not. With one membership function the algorithm is its single-Gaussian baseline; the steps cost no fitness evaluations but make a generation 8 to 17 times slower to compute. On 36 double-funnel settings the component raises the successful runs of a rank-weighted Gaussian EDA from 805 to 1712 of 1800. On the Lunacek double funnel in 30 dimensions it raises that EDA from 4 to 49 and AMaLGaM from 0 to 47 successes in 50 runs, while results on single-funnel functions and on ten multimodal BBOB functions do not change. Restarted CMA-ES remains cheaper in evaluations on the standard double funnel, and the component stops helping when the global funnel is much narrower than the other.

2611.29954.title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference
2611.29954.abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).

2611.29381.title: Gaussian Belief Propagation and Periodic Jacobi Matrices on Trees: Spectral Curve, Antibound Poles, and Fixed Points
2611.29381.abstract: Diagonal Green functions of a periodic Jacobi operator on a universal covering tree satisfy the scalar Gaussian belief propagation covariance equations on the finite connected loopless base multigraph. At cycle rank at least two, the Green functions continue to simple antibound poles at both Perron values for arbitrary real potentials and nonzero real weights. This proves the conjecture of Christiansen, Simon and Zinchenko. For positive weights the pole result includes self-loops. On loopless graphs the lower pole is the walk-summability threshold. Each energy strictly between it and the spectral bottom has at least two fixed points with positive definite local beliefs. On a connected simple graph, some coefficients yield a compact component of positive solutions exactly when the graph contains two vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of cycle rank at least two. The covariance curve is generically irreducible, with one sheet per edge subset with no vertex of degree one. For cycle rank at least two and generic real coefficients, the diagonal Green functions, infinite half-tree $m$-functions and the density-of-states Stieltjes transform all have this degree, answering a question of Avni, Breuer and Simon. Then all eigenvalues of the signed Jacobi matrices are antibound poles. Signed principal submatrices classify finite points with nonzero residue of $(\sum_i V_i) dz$, where $V_i$ are the vertex variances. We give a genus formula. Near zero potentials and unit weights on $K_4$, independently varying the coefficients leaves the cover spectrum an interval. This refutes Avni, Breuer and Simon's conjecture on the density of parameters with all gaps open. In block models, generic irreducibility and a uniqueness criterion extend, and at uniform dimension $p$ the degree can exceed $L^p$ for scalar degree $L$. Part of the scalar theory is formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

2611.29315.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
2611.29315.abstract: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincar\'e phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.

2611.29265.title: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
2611.29265.abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (~-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.

2611.29105.title: Spatial Ensemble Logic for Biomedical Imaging: Geometric Element Ensembles in Euclidean Space
2611.29105.abstract: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics over metric monoids whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We study its member over the Euclidian space, called Spatial Ensemble Logic (SEL), for biomedical images. Geometric element ensembles (GELs) represent atomic propositions by finite lists of effectively presented semi-algebraic sets, principally closed balls. Translation, dilation and erosion preserve individual balls up to emptiness in any dimension. Translation and dilation act element-wise, but element-wise erosion gives only an inner bound. For $k\geq 2$, finite unions of balls are closed under neither intersection nor erosion. We therefore separate record representation from the evaluation domain. Our main result is a satisfaction-preserving translation over GELs into the first-order theory of real closed fields. It yields computable semi-algebraic satisfaction sets, decidable model checking and finite real algebraic evidence. For a fixed formula and dimension, model checking has polynomial data complexity under stated rationality and bounded-degree assumptions. Combined complexity is PSPACE-hard and in EXPSPACE. On the line, rational interval data admit linear-arithmetic evaluation with rational evidence, under rationality assumptions on the norm, query and evaluation point. For $k\geq 2$, rational balls can force irrational witnesses. Lower and upper annotation bounds propagate through formulas. Synthesis of a ball ensemble is decidable within a prescribed budget of balls and undecidable without one. In a vascular use case, medial ball ensembles decide calibre and stenosis queries at stored centers by comparing stored numbers. We also examine how far evaluation can proceed element-wise when the union forming a support is deferred to the point of evaluation.

2611.30198.title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
2611.30198.abstract: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.

2611.28905.title: Beyond the section plane: Robust 3D reconstruction of multiplex immunofluorescence exposes limitations of 2D spatial cell statistics
2611.28905.abstract: Spatial analysis of the tumour microenvironment with multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) typically relies on single thin tissue sections, which misrepresent the 3D tissue organisation and bias spatial cell statistics in ways that remain largely unquantified. We reconstruct 24 breast and lung tumour tissue microarray cores in 3D, each from 15-20 serial mIF sections, and compare spatial cell statistics in 3D with those from individual sections. Our pipeline combines affine pre-alignment with dense deformable refinement using RoMa v2, achieving a median target registration error of 1.79 $\mu$m, well below nuclear size, which allows nuclei to be linked across sections. While cell-type proportions are preserved in 2D (Pearson corr. $r \geq 0.99$), 3D analysis reveals up to 3.8 times shorter nearest-neighbour distances, 13-19% higher neighbourhood entropy, and 2-4 times more contacts per cell. Tissue composition can thus be reliably estimated from individual sections, whereas cell-cell interactions require volumetric analysis.
